title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor
creator: early-chinese-builders
note: The vast tomb mound and underground city of Qin Shi Huang, guarded by the Terracotta Army.
description: Work on the tomb of Ying Zheng began soon after he became king of Qin in 246 BC and continued after he unified China and took the title of First Emperor in 221 BC; according to the historian Sima Qian, hundreds of thousands of conscripts laboured on it. The burial mound, originally a stepped pyramid of rammed earth now about 50 metres high, stood within two rectangular walled enclosures, the plan of a palace city for the afterlife. Sima Qian describes a burial chamber with a ceiling of heavenly bodies and rivers of mercury, and soil tests have found high mercury levels, but the central tomb has never been opened. Around it, pits discovered from 1974 contain the Terracotta Army, bronze chariots, stables and figures of officials and entertainers. The complex shows how early Chinese architecture organised space by walls, axes and hierarchy, and how much of it is now known only through tombs.
image_file: Tomb of the First Emperor Qin Shi Huang Di, Xi'an, China - panoramio.jpg
image_caption: The tomb mound of the First Emperor near Xi'an

title: Great Wall of China
creator: great-wall-builders
location: Northern China, from Shanhaiguan to Jiayuguan
note: Two thousand years of frontier walls, best known from the brick-faced Ming sections near Beijing.
description: From the seventh century BC the rival states of China built walls of rammed earth against each other and against the peoples of the steppe. After unification in 221 BC the Qin linked and extended the northern walls, and the Han pushed them far west along the Gansu corridor. Later dynasties built, neglected and rebuilt in turn; the most famous stretches, faced with brick and stone and climbing mountain ridges with watchtowers at short intervals, date from the Ming, who rebuilt the defences on a vast scale after the Mongols were driven out in 1368. The Wall was never a single continuous structure: it was a system of walls, ditches, passes, beacon towers and garrisons, and its military effectiveness is debated by historians. Its total length, including all branches and periods, was measured by a Chinese survey in 2012 at over 21,000 kilometres. Much is ruined, while sections such as Badaling and Mutianyu have been heavily restored.
image_file: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling-edit.jpg
image_caption: The Ming Great Wall at Jinshanling, Hebei

title: Mogao Caves
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
note: Nearly five hundred painted cave shrines at the Silk Road oasis of Dunhuang.
description: According to an inscription, the monk Lezun began carving the first cave into the cliff south-east of Dunhuang in 366. Over the next thousand years monks, merchants and local rulers commissioned hundreds of caves, of which 492 decorated shrines survive, together with more than 2,000 painted sculptures and some 45,000 square metres of murals. The caves range from small meditation cells to great halls with a central pillar representing a stupa and colossal Buddhas housed behind multi-storey timber facades, such as the nine-storey Jiucenglou. The murals preserve images of Tang palaces, temples and cities that no longer exist. In 1900 a sealed library cave was found containing tens of thousands of manuscripts, many later removed by foreign expeditions. The site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, is managed by the Dunhuang Academy, which limits visits to protect the fragile paintings.
image_caption: The nine-storey facade (Jiucenglou) of the Mogao Caves

title: Yungang Grottoes
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
note: Colossal Buddhas carved by the Northern Wei at their capital Pingcheng.
description: The Northern Wei, a dynasty of Xianbei origin, made Buddhism a state religion, and around 460 the monk Tanyao began carving five great caves, each with a colossal Buddha said to represent one of the dynasty's emperors, into the sandstone cliff near the capital Pingcheng, present-day Datong. Over the following decades some 250 caves and niches with more than 50,000 statues were cut along a kilometre of cliff. The early figures show strong influence from Gandhara and Central Asia, while later caves have carved imitations of timber buildings, with bracketed eaves and pagodas, which are among the best evidence for the architecture of the period. Work slowed after the court moved to Luoyang in 494. The grottoes became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.

title: Longmen Grottoes
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
note: Tens of thousands of Buddhist images cut into the limestone cliffs of the Yi River.
description: After the Northern Wei moved their capital to Luoyang in 494, carving began in the limestone cliffs on both banks of the Yi River south of the city. Work continued through the Sui and Tang dynasties, producing about 2,300 caves and niches and over 100,000 statues, with thousands of inscriptions that are a major source for the history of Chinese calligraphy. The most famous ensemble, the open-air Fengxian Temple completed in 675, centres on a Vairocana Buddha about 17 metres high, traditionally associated with the patronage of Empress Wu Zetian. Holes in the rock show that some groups were once sheltered by timber roofs. Longmen marks the shift from the elongated Northern Wei style to the full, rounded Tang ideal. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

title: Songyue Pagoda
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
note: The oldest surviving brick pagoda in China, a twelve-sided tower of fifteen eaves.
description: The Songyue Pagoda stands in a temple on Mount Song, one of China's sacred mountains, and was built around 523 under the Northern Wei. Of yellow brick bonded with clay, it rises about 37 metres from a tall base storey to fifteen closely spaced eaves that curve inward to a pointed spire, giving it a bullet-like profile. Its twelve-sided plan is unique among Chinese pagodas. The doorways and niches of the lower storey carry carved arches and lion motifs that show the Indian roots of the form. As the oldest standing brick pagoda in China, it proves how quickly Chinese builders adapted the stupa into a tower of many eaves. It forms part of the World Heritage Site of the historic monuments of Dengfeng.

title: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
location: Da Ci'en Temple, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China
note: The Tang pagoda built to house the sutras brought back from India by Xuanzang.
description: The pilgrim monk Xuanzang returned to Chang'an in 645 after sixteen years in India with hundreds of Buddhist texts, which he translated at the Da Ci'en Temple. In 652 a pagoda was built there to store them, reportedly following Xuanzang's own wishes and Indian models. That first structure of rammed earth faced with brick soon decayed, and it was rebuilt under Empress Wu Zetian around 704. The present square tower, about 64 metres high, has seven storeys of diminishing size, its brick walls modelled with flat pilasters and brackets in imitation of timber construction. Its steady, massive outline became an emblem of Xi'an. The outer brick casing was renewed in the Ming dynasty. It is part of the Silk Roads World Heritage Site.

title: Small Wild Goose Pagoda
creator: chinese-buddhist-builders
note: A slender Tang pagoda of closely stacked eaves that has survived many earthquakes.
description: The Small Wild Goose Pagoda was built between 707 and 709 at the Jianfu Temple in Chang'an, where the monk Yijing translated sutras he had brought back from India by sea. Unlike the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, it is of the multi-eaved type, with fifteen originally (now thirteen) closely spaced brick eaves on a square plan, rising in a graceful convex curve. Its height today is about 43 metres; the top storeys were lost in an earthquake in 1556. Tradition records that earlier quakes split the tower open and later closed it again, and its foundation of rammed earth shaped like a hemisphere is thought to have helped it survive. It is among the best preserved Tang brick buildings and part of the Silk Roads World Heritage Site.

title: Anji Bridge (Zhaozhou Bridge)
creator: li-chun
note: The world's oldest open-spandrel segmental stone arch bridge, still standing after fourteen centuries.
description: The Anji Bridge crosses the Xiao River at Zhao County, and a Tang inscription records that it was built by the craftsman Li Chun in the Sui dynasty. Its single arch spans about 37 metres but rises only about 7 metres, a flat segment of a circle rather than a semicircle, so that carts could cross easily. Two small arches open in each spandrel, reducing the weight of the bridge by hundreds of tonnes and letting floodwater pass through. The arch is built of 28 parallel rings of limestone blocks tied with iron cramps. The design was centuries ahead of European practice, where open-spandrel segmental arches became common only in the modern era. The bridge has been repaired many times, most heavily in the 1950s, when its balustrades were largely replaced.

title: Daxing (Sui–Tang Chang'an)
creator: yuwen-kai
note: The grid capital of the Sui and Tang, the model for capitals across East Asia.
description: In 582 Emperor Wen of the Sui ordered a new capital to be built south-east of the ruined Han city of Chang'an, and Yuwen Kai planned it with remarkable speed; the walls and palace were occupied the following year. Named Daxing by the Sui and Chang'an by the Tang, the city formed a rectangle about 9.7 by 8.6 kilometres enclosed by rammed-earth walls. The palace and the government city lay at the north centre; a broad avenue some 150 metres wide ran south from them to the main gate, and the rest of the city was divided into walled residential wards and two great markets. With perhaps a million inhabitants under the Tang, it was the largest city in the world and a meeting place of merchants, monks and envoys from across Asia. The plan was copied in Japan at Nara and Kyoto. The city was largely destroyed at the end of the Tang, and little survives above ground apart from its pagodas; its gate towers are known from tomb murals.
image_caption: Mural of gate towers in the tomb of the Tang prince Li Chongrun (Prince Yide), 706

title: Great Buddha Hall of Nanchan Temple
creator: tang-carpenters
note: The oldest dated timber building in China, a small hall that escaped the persecution of Buddhism in 845.
description: The main hall of Nanchan Temple, on the slopes of the sacred Buddhist mountain Wutai, carries an inscription on a beam recording its rebuilding in 782. It is a modest hall of three bays by three under a hipped and gabled roof, with no interior columns, so that the roof is carried entirely by a frame of beams and bracket sets resting on the outer columns. Its small size and remote location probably saved it during the great persecution of Buddhism in 845, when thousands of temples were destroyed. The hall still contains a group of Tang clay sculptures on a platform. It was identified by Chinese researchers in the 1950s and restored in the 1970s, when later alterations were removed to bring it closer to its Tang form.
image_caption: Great Buddha Hall of Nanchan Temple

title: East Hall of Foguang Temple
creator: tang-carpenters
note: The largest surviving Tang timber hall, rediscovered by Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin in 1937.
description: Foguang Temple was rebuilt after the persecution of 845, and its East Hall, completed in 857, was paid for by a woman donor named Ning Gongyu, whose name Lin Huiyin found inscribed on a roof beam. The hall is seven bays wide and four deep, raised on a terrace on the hillside. Its powerful bracket sets, nearly half the height of the columns, carry deep eaves that project about four metres, and the interior combines an outer ring of columns and an inner ring around a platform crowded with Tang sculptures. In 1937 Liang Sicheng, Lin Huiyin and colleagues reached the temple by mule, guided by a Dunhuang mural that showed it, and identified it as a Tang building, then the only one known. Their survey made the hall the classic example of Tang timber architecture and confirmed the system described in later manuals. It is part of the Mount Wutai World Heritage Site.

title: Guanyin Pavilion of Dule Temple
creator: liao-song-builders
note: A two-storey Liao timber pavilion built around a sixteen-metre statue of Guanyin.
description: Dule Temple was rebuilt in 984 under the Liao, a Khitan dynasty ruling northern China, and its Guanyin Pavilion is one of the oldest surviving multi-storey timber buildings in China. From outside it appears to have two storeys, but inside a hidden mezzanine makes three structural levels, rising around a central void that holds a clay statue of the eleven-headed Guanyin about 16 metres tall, one of the largest of its kind. Twenty-four different types of bracket sets tie the frame together. The pavilion survived numerous earthquakes, including a strong one in 1679 that destroyed most buildings in the area. Liang Sicheng surveyed it in 1932, his first major field study, and called it a key link between Tang and Song architecture.

title: Pagoda of Fogong Temple (Yingxian Wooden Pagoda)
creator: liao-song-builders
note: The oldest and tallest fully wooden pagoda in the world, a Liao masterpiece about 67 metres high.
description: The Shijia Pagoda of Fogong Temple was built in 1056 by the Liao emperor Daozong on the site of his grandmother's family home. Octagonal in plan, it shows five storeys outside but has four hidden mezzanines, making nine structural levels, each a ring of columns linked by beams and stiffened by diagonal bracing. Some fifty-four different kinds of bracket sets have been counted. Each main storey houses Buddhist statues, and inside the pagoda relics and printed sutras of the Liao were found during repairs in the 1970s. Its height of about 67 metres makes it the tallest pre-modern timber building in China. It has survived earthquakes and war damage but now leans, and the best way to stabilise it has been debated by engineers for decades.
image_caption: Pagoda of Fogong Temple, Ying County

title: Longxing Temple
creator: liao-song-builders
note: A Northern Song temple with a unique cross-shaped hall and a colossal bronze Guanyin.
description: Longxing Temple was founded under the Sui in 586, but its present buildings date mainly from the Northern Song. The Hall of Manichudana (Moni Hall), built in 1052, has a square core with porticoes projecting from each side, giving a cross-shaped plan with gable fronts that is known from Song paintings but survives nowhere else. Further back, the Pavilion of Great Mercy houses a bronze Guanyin with forty-two arms, about 21 metres tall, cast in 971 on the orders of the first Song emperor. The temple also preserves a rare revolving sutra cabinet in its own pavilion. Liang Sicheng surveyed it in 1933 and considered the Moni Hall one of the most important examples of Song architecture.

title: Hall of the Holy Mother, Jinci
creator: liao-song-builders
note: A Song dynasty hall with dragon-wrapped columns, set among the springs of an ancient shrine.
description: Jinci is a complex of shrines at the source of the Jin River south-west of Taiyuan, dedicated to the founder of the ancient state of Jin. Its centrepiece, the Hall of the Holy Mother, honours his mother and was built under the Northern Song between 1023 and 1032 and repaired in 1102. The hall has a double-eaved roof and a deep open portico at the front, whose eight columns are encircled by carved wooden dragons, the oldest of their kind. Inside, the absence of interior columns creates a single space for some forty painted clay figures of court ladies, eunuchs and attendants, celebrated for their lifelike individual expressions. In front of the hall, a cross-shaped bridge over a fish pond is also of Song date.
image_caption: Hall of the Holy Mother, Jinci

title: Iron Pagoda of Kaifeng
creator: liao-song-builders
note: A Song pagoda clad in iron-coloured glazed tiles, in the old Northern Song capital.
description: The pagoda of Youguo Temple in Kaifeng was built in 1049 to replace a timber pagoda destroyed by lightning. It is octagonal, with thirteen storeys rising about 55 metres, and is faced with brown glazed tiles moulded with Buddhas, flying celestials, lions and floral patterns; their dark colour gave it the name Iron Pagoda. The brick walls imitate timber posts, beams and brackets. Kaifeng was repeatedly flooded by the Yellow River, and the pagoda's base now lies buried beneath silt. It survived these floods, earthquakes and shelling in 1938, and is one of the finest examples of the use of glazed ceramic in Song architecture.

title: Yingzao Fashi
creator: li-jie
note: The Song court's illustrated treatise on building standards, the key text of Chinese architectural history.
description: The Yingzao Fashi ('Treatise on Architectural Methods' or 'State Building Standards') was compiled by Li Jie of the Directorate of Buildings and Construction and printed in 1103 to control costs and standardise imperial building. Its thirty-four chapters cover terminology, foundations, stone, carpentry, joinery, carving, painting, tiling and brickwork, with labour quotas and material estimates, and six chapters of illustrations of bracket sets, cross-sections and decorative patterns. Its central principle is a modular unit, the cai, defined by the section of a standard bracket arm, with eight grades for buildings of different rank, so that all dimensions followed from the building's status. Only later copies survive, and the text was long almost unreadable. A copy found in 1919 was published, and Liang Sicheng spent much of his career decoding it by comparing it with surviving buildings.
image_caption: Page of the Yingzao Fashi showing bracket sets

title: Forbidden City
creator: kuai-xiang
note: The palace of the Ming and Qing emperors, the largest surviving ensemble of traditional timber architecture.
description: When the Yongle Emperor moved the Ming capital to Beijing, he ordered a new palace built on the site of the Yuan palace; construction ran from 1406 to 1420, using timber floated from the south-west and stone and bricks from across northern China. The rectangular walled precinct, about 960 by 750 metres and surrounded by a moat, contains some 980 buildings. It is laid out along a north–south axis: an outer court of three great halls on a triple marble terrace, led by the Hall of Supreme Harmony, for state ceremonies, and an inner court of residential palaces and a garden for the emperor and his household. Yellow glazed roofs, red walls and the number and form of roofs and ornaments express the strict hierarchy of the empire. Most halls have been rebuilt after fires, many in the Qing. Twenty-four emperors lived there until 1912; since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum. Kuai Xiang is traditionally credited with its design, though it was the work of an imperial bureaucracy.
image_file: The Forbidden City - View from Coal Hill.jpg
image_caption: The Forbidden City seen from Jingshan (Coal Hill)

title: Tiananmen
creator: kuai-xiang
note: The 'Gate of Heavenly Peace', front gate of the imperial city and symbol of the People's Republic.
description: The gate first built in 1420 as the Chengtian Gate, the main southern entrance to the Imperial City in front of the Forbidden City, is traditionally attributed to the master carpenter Kuai Xiang. It was destroyed in fighting at the fall of the Ming in 1644 and rebuilt under the Qing in 1651 with its present name. A gate tower of nine bays by five, under a double-eaved hipped and gabled roof of yellow tiles, stands on a massive red platform pierced by five arched passages, the central one reserved for the emperor. Imperial edicts were proclaimed from its balcony. On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic there, and the gate appears on the national emblem designed by Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin's team. It was entirely reconstructed in 1969–70 to the old design.

title: Temple of Heaven
creator: ming-imperial-builders
note: The altars where Ming and Qing emperors offered sacrifices to Heaven, with the circular Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests.
description: The Temple of Heaven was built in the same years as the Forbidden City, south-east of it in the outer city of Beijing, and was enlarged in the sixteenth century. Its precinct, larger than the palace, is enclosed by a wall rounded at the north and square at the south, reflecting the ancient idea of a round Heaven over a square Earth. Along a raised causeway lie the open-air Circular Mound Altar, of three white marble tiers where the emperor sacrificed at the winter solstice, the Imperial Vault of Heaven, and the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, a round hall with a triple roof of blue tiles on a three-tiered marble terrace. Its timber frame of concentric rings of columns symbolises the seasons, months and hours. The hall burned after a lightning strike in 1889 and was rebuilt to the old design. The complex is a World Heritage Site and the supreme expression of Chinese ritual architecture.
image_caption: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, Temple of Heaven

title: Ming Tombs
creator: ming-imperial-builders
note: The burial valley of thirteen Ming emperors, approached by a Spirit Way of stone figures.
description: In 1409 the Yongle Emperor chose a valley north of Beijing, sheltered by mountains on three sides according to principles of geomancy, for his tomb, and thirteen of the sixteen Ming emperors were later buried there. A single approach serves the whole necropolis: a stone archway of 1540, a great red gate and a Spirit Way lined with pairs of stone animals and officials. Each tomb follows the same plan of a sacrificial hall in front of a walled, tree-covered burial mound. Yongle's Changling has the largest surviving hall, the Hall of Eminent Favour, supported by huge columns of single nanmu tree trunks. The underground palace of the Wanli Emperor's Dingling was excavated in the 1950s, but poor conservation damaged its contents, and no further tombs have been opened. The Ming and Qing imperial tombs are a World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Great Red Gate at the entrance to the Ming Tombs

title: Summer Palace
creator: lei-family
note: The Qing imperial garden of Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill, rebuilt for the Empress Dowager Cixi.
description: The Qianlong Emperor created the Garden of Clear Ripples in 1750 around a hill and an enlarged lake north-west of Beijing, in honour of his mother's birthday. Burned by British and French troops in 1860, it was rebuilt from 1886, reportedly with funds diverted from the navy, for the Empress Dowager Cixi, and renamed Yiheyuan, the 'Garden of Preserved Harmony'; it was damaged again in 1900 and repaired. The court designers of the Lei family prepared plans and models for the reconstruction. The design borrows scenes from across China, especially from the lakes of Hangzhou and the gardens of the south: the Tower of Buddhist Incense crowns Longevity Hill, a painted Long Corridor of over 700 metres runs along the shore, and causeways, a seventeen-arch bridge and a marble boat dot the lake. It is a World Heritage Site and the best preserved Chinese imperial garden.
image_file: Longevity Hill of the Summer Palace.jpg
image_caption: Longevity Hill and the Tower of Buddhist Incense, Summer Palace

title: Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan)
creator: lei-family
note: The vast Qing garden palace, with European-style pavilions by Jesuits, destroyed in 1860.
description: The Yuanmingyuan, the 'Garden of Perfect Brightness', began as a gift from the Kangxi Emperor to his son, the future Yongzheng Emperor, in 1707, and grew under the Qianlong Emperor into a complex of three gardens covering about 350 hectares, with hundreds of halls, pavilions and scenes around lakes and canals. The emperors lived and governed there for much of the year. The Lei family served as court designers for many of its buildings. In one corner Jesuit missionaries, among them Giuseppe Castiglione, designed the Xiyang Lou, Western-style palaces of stone with fountains and mazes. In October 1860, during the Second Opium War, British and French troops looted the palace and the British commander ordered it burned. Further destruction followed. The ruins of the European buildings are now its best-known image, and the site has become a memorial to national humiliation.
image_caption: Ruins of the Great Fountain (Dashuifa), Yuanmingyuan

title: Chengde Mountain Resort and Outlying Temples
creator: qing-imperial-builders
note: The Qing summer capital beyond the Great Wall, with temples modelled on Tibetan monasteries.
description: The Kangxi Emperor began a summer palace at Chengde, north-east of Beijing beyond the Great Wall, in 1703, and the Qianlong Emperor enlarged it until 1792. The resort, enclosed by a wall about ten kilometres long, combines restrained grey-tiled palace halls, lakes with scenes copied from southern gardens, a plain and a mountainous park. It was used for hunting and for receiving Mongol, Tibetan and other envoys of the multi-ethnic empire. Around it the emperors built a ring of Buddhist temples in Chinese, Tibetan and mixed styles, including the Putuo Zongcheng Temple (1771), modelled on the Potala Palace in Lhasa, and the Xumi Fushou Temple based on the Tashilhunpo monastery. The ensemble is a World Heritage Site and shows how Qing architecture expressed political rule over Inner Asia.

title: Potala Palace
creator: tibetan-builders
note: The Tibetan palace-fortress of the Dalai Lamas on the Red Hill of Lhasa.
description: The Potala belongs to the Tibetan, not the Chinese, building tradition. The Fifth Dalai Lama began it in 1645 on the site of a seventh-century palace of the king Songtsen Gampo, and the White Palace, his residence and seat of government, was finished in 1648; the central Red Palace, containing chapels and the gilded tombs of Dalai Lamas, was completed in 1694. The complex climbs the hill to a height of over 110 metres, with thick, inward-sloping walls of stone and rammed earth, small windows and flat roofs, crowned by gilded pavilion roofs. It contains more than a thousand rooms. The Dalai Lamas lived there until the fourteenth fled into exile in 1959. Now a museum, it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1994; the Qing emperors copied its form at Chengde.

title: Humble Administrator's Garden
creator: suzhou-garden-makers
note: The largest classical garden of Suzhou, a sequence of ponds, islands and pavilions.
description: The garden was created from about 1509 by Wang Xianchen, a censor who retired to Suzhou after a troubled career; its name alludes to a line by the Jin poet Pan Yue about the retired man's simple life of tending a garden as the 'administration' of a humble man. The painter Wen Zhengming, a friend of Wang, painted and described its views in an album of 1533, and he is often said to have helped design it, though this is uncertain. The garden has since been divided, sold and rebuilt many times; its present form largely dates from the nineteenth century. Covering about five hectares, it is mostly water, with islands, zigzag bridges, halls and galleries arranged so that views open and close in sequence, and borrows the distant North Temple Pagoda as part of its scenery. It is one of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou on the World Heritage list.

title: Lingering Garden
creator: suzhou-garden-makers
note: A Suzhou garden of courtyards and corridors, famous for its towering Guanyun Peak rock.
description: The Lingering Garden was begun in 1593 by the official Xu Taishi as the East Garden, and after changes of ownership was rebuilt in the nineteenth century, taking its present name under the Sheng family. It is known for its sophisticated sequence of spaces: from a narrow, dim entrance passage the visitor moves through small courtyards and lattice windows into a central pond and hill garden, and then to eastern courtyards of halls and rocks. Long covered corridors, their walls pierced by windows with different lattice patterns, frame changing views. The Crown of Clouds Peak (Guanyun feng), a tall perforated Lake Tai rock about 6.5 metres high, is one of the most celebrated garden stones in China. It is part of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou World Heritage Site.

title: Master of the Nets Garden
creator: suzhou-garden-makers
note: A small residential garden prized as the most perfectly proportioned of Suzhou's gardens.
description: A garden called the Fisherman's Retreat was made on this site by a Song dynasty official, and in the 1770s the retired official Song Zongyuan rebuilt it, choosing the name 'Master of the Nets' with its ideal of a hermit fisherman. Later owners added to it. It is compact, about half a hectare, and integrated with the family residence: a series of halls and courtyards leads to a central pond around which buildings, rockeries and a covered walkway are arranged at a carefully judged scale, so that the small space seems larger. A courtyard of the garden served as the model for the Astor Court built in 1981 at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. It is one of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou World Heritage Site.
image_file: Master of the Nets Garden Suzhou.jpg
image_caption: Master of the Nets Garden, Suzhou

title: Yu Garden
creator: suzhou-garden-makers
note: A Ming garden in the old walled city of Shanghai, built by an official for his parents.
description: The official Pan Yunduan began the Yu Garden, the 'Garden of Pleasing', in 1559 to give his aged parents a pleasant retreat, completing it around 1577. Its great rockery of yellow stones is attributed to the noted rockery maker Zhang Nanyang. The garden decayed after the Pan family declined, was restored by merchants in the eighteenth century and was damaged in the Opium War and the Taiping rebellion, then restored again from the 1950s. Today it covers about two hectares of halls, ponds, rockeries and pavilions divided by walls topped with undulating dragons. The surrounding streets have been rebuilt as a bazaar in traditional style, and the garden is one of the most visited sights of Shanghai.

title: Yuanye (The Craft of Gardens)
creator: ji-cheng
location: Printed in the lower Yangzi region
note: The only classical Chinese treatise devoted wholly to the design and construction of gardens.
description: Ji Cheng wrote the Yuanye after decades of building gardens for officials in the Yangzi delta, and it was printed in 1634 with prefaces by friends and patrons. In three books it discusses the choice of site, the types of buildings, railings, doors and windows, walls, paving, rockeries and the selection of stones, with diagrams of lattice and paving patterns. Ji Cheng insisted that a garden should be adapted to its site and that the designer, not the builders, determines its quality. He gave a famous name to the practice of 'borrowing scenery' (jiejing), incorporating views beyond the walls. Written in elegant parallel prose, the book was hardly known in China after the Ming, partly because of its association with the disgraced Ruan Dacheng, but survived in Japan and was republished in China in the 1930s. It is now a classic of garden history.

title: Fujian Tulou
creator: vernacular-builders
note: Massive round and square earthen houses built by Hakka and other clans for whole communities.
description: In the mountains of south-western Fujian, Hakka and Minnan clans built tulou, fortified houses of rammed earth that could hold several hundred people of one lineage. Most surviving examples date from the seventeenth to the twentieth centuries. A typical round tulou has outer walls of earth up to two metres thick at the base, with no windows on the lower floors and a single gate, enclosing a ring of three or four storeys of identical family rooms, built of timber, opening on to galleries that face a courtyard with an ancestral hall at the centre. Square, oval and other forms also occur. The design combined defence against bandits with an egalitarian distribution of space. In 2008 forty-six tulou were inscribed as a World Heritage Site, and groups such as the Tianluokeng cluster of four round houses and one square one are now well known.

image_caption: Tianluokeng tulou cluster, Nanjing County, Fujian

title: Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum
creator: lu-yanzhi
note: The tomb of the founder of the Chinese Republic, a modern monument in Chinese form.
description: Sun Yat-sen died in 1925 having asked to be buried on Purple Mountain outside Nanjing. An international competition was held, and Lü Yanzhi's design won; construction began in 1926 and Sun's body was interred in 1929, although work continued into the early 1930s and Lü himself died before it was complete. The mausoleum is approached through a memorial arch and a gate, then up a broad stairway of 392 steps rising about 70 metres to a memorial hall of white granite with a blue-tiled roof, in reinforced concrete. Behind it lies a domed chamber with a marble effigy of Sun above the burial vault. The plan, seen from above, was said to resemble a bell, an image of awakening the nation. The mausoleum became the model for the Nationalist government's 'Chinese renaissance' architecture and is one of the most visited sites in China.

title: Monument to the People's Heroes
creator: liang-sicheng
note: The granite obelisk at the centre of Tiananmen Square, designed by a team led by Liang Sicheng.
description: In 1949 the new government decided to raise a monument to those who had died in the revolutionary struggles of the previous century, and a design committee was formed that included Liang Sicheng as a leading designer and Lin Huiyin, who was responsible for much of the decorative design. Built from 1952 and unveiled in 1958, it is a granite obelisk about 38 metres high, standing on a two-tiered terrace with white marble balustrades. The front carries an inscription in Mao Zedong's calligraphy, and the base is surrounded by eight large marble reliefs depicting events from the Opium War to the crossing of the Yangzi in 1949. Liang argued for a monument with a traditional Chinese character, a stele rather than a Western obelisk, and the result combines both. The monument has been a focus of mourning and protest, notably in 1976 and 1989.
