image_caption: Monument to the People's Heroes, Tiananmen Square

title: Bank of China Tower
creator: pei
note: I. M. Pei's triangulated glass tower, for a time the tallest building in Asia.
description: The Bank of China commissioned I. M. Pei, whose father had been a senior figure at the bank, to design its Hong Kong headquarters, completed in 1990 ahead of the return of Hong Kong to China. The tower is a square in plan divided diagonally into four triangular prisms that terminate at different heights, so that the building narrows as it rises to 315 metres (367 metres with its masts). Its structure is a space frame of steel and concrete with giant diagonal braces expressed on the facade, which allowed it to use much less steel than conventional towers of its height. The design was inspired by the image of growing bamboo. Its sharp edges were criticised by some local practitioners of feng shui. It was the tallest building in Asia until 1992 and remains a defining element of the Hong Kong skyline.
image_caption: Bank of China Tower, Hong Kong

title: Suzhou Museum
creator: pei
note: Pei's late homage to the gardens of his ancestral city, beside the Humble Administrator's Garden.
description: In his late eighties I. M. Pei accepted the commission for a new museum of Suzhou's art and history, next to the Humble Administrator's Garden and in the city where his family had lived for generations. The museum, opened in 2006, takes the white plastered walls and grey roofs of local houses and translates them into crisp geometry, with roofs of dark grey granite, steel frames and skylights that filter light through wooden louvres. Galleries are arranged around courtyards and a central garden with a pond, a bridge and a 'rock painting' of sliced stones set against a white wall, a modern reinterpretation of the garden rockery. Pei described it as his 'little daughter', and it is often considered one of the most successful attempts to create a modern Chinese architecture.
image_file: 苏州博物馆·苏州·西南向东北.jpg

title: Ningbo Museum
creator: wang-shu
note: A mountain-like museum clad in bricks and tiles salvaged from demolished villages.
description: The Ningbo Museum (Ningbo History Museum) was built in a new district of the city where the old villages had been cleared. Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu of Amateur Architecture Studio designed it as a massive block that splits at the top into a fractured, mountain-like silhouette, with irregular openings and inner courtyards and valleys. Its walls are built partly in the wapan technique of local builders, with reused bricks and tiles of many sizes and dates laid in a dense, varied mosaic, and partly in concrete cast in bamboo formwork. Some two million salvaged pieces were used. Opened in 2008, the museum was cited when Wang received the Pritzker Prize in 2012 as an example of his concern for memory and craft in a period of rapid destruction.

title: Xiangshan Campus, China Academy of Art
creator: wang-shu
note: Wang Shu's campus of buildings in recycled tile and rammed earth, set among farmland and hills.
description: For the new campus of the China Academy of Art at Xiangshan, on the outskirts of Hangzhou, Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu designed a group of buildings in two phases between 2002 and 2007. Instead of a monumental plan, they arranged the buildings informally around a small hill, keeping fields, ponds and streams between them as in a village. More than seven million old tiles and bricks salvaged from demolished buildings in the region were used for walls and roofs, together with bamboo, timber and rammed earth, and the roofs and walkways were shaped with reference to Chinese landscape painting. The campus became the main manifesto of Wang's idea of an architecture rooted in craft and local memory, and he heads the architecture school housed there.

title: Ise Grand Shrine
creator: shinto-shrine-builders
year: form from late 7th century; rebuilt every 20 years, most recently 2013
note: Japan's most sacred shrine, rebuilt in identical form every twenty years for some thirteen centuries.
description: Ise Jingū consists of two main shrines, the Inner Shrine (Naikū) dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu, ancestor of the imperial line, and the Outer Shrine (Gekū) dedicated to Toyouke, goddess of food, together with more than a hundred smaller shrines. The main sanctuaries are built in the shinmei-zukuri style: raised floors, unpainted cypress, thatched gable roofs crowned by crossed finials (chigi) and short logs (katsuogi), and freestanding posts carrying the ridge, forms that recall ancient granaries. Every twenty years, in the ceremony of shikinen sengū, the sanctuaries and many other buildings are rebuilt on an adjacent plot and the old ones dismantled, a tradition dating back, according to shrine records, to 690. The sixty-second rebuilding took place in 2013. The practice preserves not the material but the form and the skills of carpenters, and it led modern architects such as Bruno Taut and Kenzō Tange to see Ise as an archetype of Japanese architecture. The innermost precincts may not be entered by the public.

title: Izumo Taisha
creator: shinto-shrine-builders
note: One of Japan's oldest shrines, whose main hall preserves the ancient taisha-zukuri style.
description: Izumo Taisha is dedicated to Ōkuninushi, a god of the land, of marriage and good relations, and appears in the eighth-century chronicles Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Its main hall (honden) is built in the taisha-zukuri style, regarded as one of the oldest forms of shrine architecture: a square plan of two by two bays with a central pillar, an entrance at one side of the gable end and a steep, curved roof of cypress bark. The present hall, of 1744, is about 24 metres tall, the largest of its kind, but shrine legends describe much taller halls of the past, raised on long stilts. In 2000 excavations found the bases of giant columns, each made of three tree trunks bound together, from a thirteenth-century rebuilding, lending weight to these traditions. The main hall is periodically re-roofed, most recently in 2013, and is a National Treasure.

title: Itsukushima Shrine
creator: shinto-shrine-builders
note: A shrine built on piers over a tidal inlet, with a great torii standing in the sea.
description: The island of Itsukushima (Miyajima) in the Inland Sea was considered sacred, and a shrine to three sea goddesses is recorded there from the sixth century. Its present plan was created in 1168 by Taira no Kiyomori, the dominant warrior statesman of the age, who made it his family shrine. The halls, painted vermilion and linked by long corridors, stand on piers over the tidal flats, so that at high tide the shrine seems to float, and its arrangement echoes the shinden-zukuri palace style of the Heian aristocracy. The buildings were rebuilt after fires in the thirteenth century and later, and include a Noh stage. The great torii in the sea, about 16 metres high, dates in its present form from 1875. The shrine became a World Heritage Site in 1996 and is one of Japan's most famous views.
image_caption: The great torii of Itsukushima Shrine

title: Hōryū-ji
creator: asuka-nara-builders
note: The temple of Prince Shōtoku, whose golden hall and pagoda are the oldest surviving timber buildings in the world.
description: Hōryū-ji was founded in 607 by Prince Shōtoku and Empress Suiko. According to the Nihon Shoki it burned down in 670, and its western precinct was rebuilt by the early eighth century, though the exact dates and whether parts survive from the first temple are long-standing scholarly debates. Its golden hall (kondō) and five-storey pagoda stand side by side within a cloister entered through a middle gate, an asymmetrical arrangement unlike Chinese practice. The buildings show features of the Chinese style of the sixth and seventh centuries, transmitted through Korea: swelling columns, cloud-shaped brackets and railings with swastika patterns. Tree-ring dating has shown that the pagoda's central pillar was felled in 594. The eastern precinct includes the octagonal Yumedono (739). A fire in 1949 that damaged the golden hall's murals led to Japan's Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties. In 1993 Hōryū-ji became, with Himeji Castle, one of Japan's first World Heritage Sites.
image_caption: Golden hall and pagoda of Hōryū-ji

title: East Pagoda of Yakushi-ji
creator: asuka-nara-builders
note: A three-storey pagoda whose intermediate skirt roofs give it a rhythm of six roofs.
description: Yakushi-ji was founded by Emperor Tenmu in 680, who vowed it for the recovery of his consort, the future Empress Jitō, and was moved to the new capital Heijō-kyō (Nara) after 710. Its East Pagoda, dated to 730, is the only building to survive from the Nara period temple. It has three main storeys, each with a smaller pent roof (mokoshi) below, so that it appears to have six roofs of alternating size, a lively rhythm that is often described as frozen music. A bronze finial at the top carries openwork flying celestials. The West Pagoda, burned in 1528, was rebuilt in 1981 in bright Tang colours, showing how the East Pagoda may once have looked. The East Pagoda underwent a full dismantling and restoration completed in 2020. Yakushi-ji is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site.

title: Tōdai-ji
creator: asuka-nara-builders
note: The great state temple of Nara, whose Great Buddha Hall was long the largest timber building in the world.
description: In 743 Emperor Shōmu ordered the casting of a colossal bronze Buddha, Vairocana, as the centre of a national network of temples, and the image was consecrated in 752 in a ceremony attended by monks from across Asia. The Great Buddha Hall (Daibutsuden) that sheltered it was flanked by two seven-storey pagodas. The temple was burned in 1180 during the Genpei War and rebuilt under the monk Chōgen, then burned again in fighting in 1567. The present hall, completed in 1709, is about 57 metres wide, roughly a third narrower than the original, but still one of the largest timber buildings in the world; its enormous roof beams required giant pines found with difficulty. The Shōsōin storehouse, the Hokke-dō with its eighth-century sculptures and Chōgen's Great South Gate also survive. Tōdai-ji is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site.

title: Golden Hall of Tōshōdai-ji
creator: asuka-nara-builders
note: The only surviving golden hall of the Nara period, in the temple of the Chinese monk Ganjin.
description: Tōshōdai-ji was founded in 759 by Ganjin (Jianzhen), a Chinese monk who reached Japan in 753 after five failed voyages and the loss of his sight, to train Japanese monks in the proper rules of ordination. Its golden hall (kondō), built in the late eighth century after his death, is the only main hall of a Nara temple to survive from the period. Seven bays wide, it has an open colonnade along the front, a single great hipped roof and three-stepped bracket sets, and houses large dry-lacquer and wooden statues of Vairocana, the Healing Buddha and a thousand-armed Kannon. The roof was made steeper in later repairs. Between 2000 and 2009 the hall was completely dismantled and rebuilt using its original timbers. Tōshōdai-ji is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site.

title: Shōsōin
creator: asuka-nara-builders
note: A raised log storehouse that has preserved the treasures of Emperor Shōmu for more than twelve centuries.
description: After Emperor Shōmu's death in 756 his widow, Empress Kōmyō, dedicated his personal possessions to the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, and they were placed in this storehouse. The building is raised on forty tall wooden posts and its walls are built in the azekura technique of horizontal logs of triangular section, interlocked at the corners, under a single hipped roof. It is divided into three sections. The collection, some 9,000 objects including musical instruments, mirrors, textiles, glass and documents from China, Persia and Central Asia as well as Japan, has survived in remarkable condition. The treasures were moved to modern fireproof storehouses in the twentieth century; a selection is shown each autumn at the Nara National Museum. The building, administered by the Imperial Household Agency, is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site.

title: Phoenix Hall of Byōdō-in
creator: heian-builders
note: The Amida hall of Fujiwara no Yorimichi, an image of the Pure Land rising over a pond.
description: Byōdō-in was a villa of the regent Fujiwara no Michinaga that his son Yorimichi converted into a temple in 1052, the year many believed the age of the 'decline of the Dharma' had begun. The Amida Hall, dedicated in 1053, houses a gilded wooden statue of the Buddha Amida by the sculptor Jōchō, surrounded by carved celestial musicians on the walls. The hall stands on an island in a pond, with a central pavilion flanked by L-shaped wings on raised corridors and a tail corridor at the back, a shape later likened to a bird with outspread wings; bronze phoenixes stand on the ridge, giving it the name Hōōdō. Seen across the water, it was meant to evoke Amida's palace in the Western Paradise. The hall survived the wars that destroyed most of Kyoto and appears on the ten-yen coin. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

title: Konjikidō of Chūson-ji
creator: heian-builders
note: A small hall covered in gold leaf, lacquer and mother-of-pearl, mausoleum of the northern Fujiwara.
description: In the early twelfth century Fujiwara no Kiyohira, ruler of the northern frontier region, built at his capital Hiraizumi a group of temples to rival those of Kyoto. The Konjikidō, or Golden Hall, completed in 1124, is a square hall of only about 5.5 metres a side, its interior and exterior covered with gold leaf over black lacquer and its altars inlaid with mother-of-pearl from the southern seas and decorated with gilt bronze. Beneath the altars lie the mummified remains of Kiyohira and the three succeeding lords of the family. A protective enclosing hall was built over it in the thirteenth century; the present concrete shelter, with the hall behind glass, dates from 1965. It is the most opulent surviving work of late Heian architecture and part of the Hiraizumi World Heritage Site.

title: Sanjūsangen-dō
creator: heian-builders
note: A hall about 120 metres long housing a thousand and one statues of Kannon.
description: Rengeō-in, known as Sanjūsangen-dō, the 'hall of thirty-three bays', was built in 1164 by Taira no Kiyomori for the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa. It burned in 1249 and was rebuilt in 1266. The hall is about 120 metres long, the longest timber building in Japan, with a single row of thirty-three bays between its columns. Inside stand a seated thousand-armed Kannon by the sculptor Tankei and a thousand standing Kannon statues in ranks, many made in the thirteenth century by sculptors of the Kei school. The long veranda was used from the Edo period for an archery contest in which archers shot along its full length. The building, a National Treasure, shows the late Heian style in its simplest monumental form.

title: Great South Gate (Nandaimon) of Tōdai-ji
creator: chogen
note: Chōgen's colossal gate in the 'Great Buddha style', guarded by Unkei and Kaikei's Niō statues.
description: The Great South Gate was raised in 1199 as part of Chōgen's reconstruction of Tōdai-ji and completed in 1203. About 25 metres high, it uses the Daibutsuyō ('Great Buddha style') that Chōgen introduced from southern China: eighteen tall columns run straight up to the roof, tied together by horizontal penetrating tie-beams, and bracket arms are inserted directly into the columns in six steps to carry the deep eaves. There is no ceiling, so the whole structure is visible from below. The method allowed a huge gate to be built quickly and economically. In 1203 the sculptors Unkei and Kaikei and their workshop carved the two Kongō Rikishi guardian figures, each about 8.4 metres tall, in only sixty-nine days. The gate and statues are National Treasures and among the most powerful works of Kamakura architecture and sculpture.

title: Shariden of Engaku-ji
creator: zen-temple-builders
note: The finest surviving example of the Chinese 'Zen style' in Japan.
description: Engaku-ji was founded in 1282 by the regent Hōjō Tokimune for the Chinese Chan master Wuxue Zuyuan (Mugaku Sogen), in memory of those who died fighting the Mongol invasions. Its relic hall (Shariden), traditionally said to house a tooth of the Buddha, is a small building of the fifteenth century, moved to Engaku-ji from another temple. It is the classic example of the Zenshūyō or 'Zen style' adopted from Song China: a steep thatched roof with sharply upturned corners above a pent roof, closely set bracket sets including between the columns, rafters fanning out at the corners, cusped bell-shaped windows (katōmado) and panelled doors. It is a National Treasure and is usually open to the public only on a few days a year.

title: Saihō-ji (Moss Temple)
creator: muso-soseki
note: Musō Soseki's two-level garden, now carpeted in more than a hundred kinds of moss.
description: Saihō-ji was an old temple of the Pure Land school that Musō Soseki restored as a Zen temple in 1339. He reshaped its garden into two parts. The lower garden is a strolling garden around a pond shaped like the character for heart (kokoro), with islands and pavilions. The upper garden, on the hillside, contains an arrangement of rocks that forms a dry waterfall, often regarded as one of the earliest examples of the dry landscape (karesansui) garden. The Ashikaga shōguns Yoshimitsu and Yoshimasa admired it and modelled their own gardens on it. The moss for which it is now famous grew in later centuries after the buildings decayed and the garden was flooded. To protect it, visits are by advance application, with copying of sutras before the tour. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.
image_file: Matsuojingatanicho, Nishikyo Ward, Kyoto, Kyoto Prefecture 615-8286, Japan - panoramio (1).jpg

title: Garden of Tenryū-ji
creator: muso-soseki
note: The Sōgenchi pond garden laid out by Musō Soseki, with a dry waterfall and borrowed mountain scenery.
description: Tenryū-ji was founded in 1339 by the shōgun Ashikaga Takauji to console the spirit of Emperor Go-Daigo, whom he had defeated, and Musō Soseki was its founding abbot; trading ships were sent to China to help pay for it. The temple buildings have burned many times and most date from the Meiji period, but the Sōgenchi pond garden behind the abbot's quarters is thought to preserve Musō's design. A pond with a beach of pebbles lies beneath a composition of tall stones on the far shore that represents a waterfall and a carp climbing it, a Chinese image of enlightenment, with a stone bridge before it. The hills of Arashiyama form a borrowed background. Tenryū-ji was ranked first among Kyoto's Five Mountain Zen temples and is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

title: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
creator: zen-temple-builders
note: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's gilded relic pavilion over a pond, rebuilt after arson in 1950.
description: In 1397 the retired shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu acquired an aristocratic estate in the northern hills of Kyoto and built a villa, which became the Zen temple Rokuon-ji after his death in 1408. Its three-storey pavilion stands at the edge of a pond: the first floor is in the style of an aristocratic palace, the second in the style of a warrior residence and the third in the form of a Zen Buddhist hall with cusped windows, and the upper two storeys are covered in gold leaf. The pavilion, which housed relics of the Buddha, survived until 1950, when a young monk burned it down, an event that inspired Yukio Mishima's novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. It was rebuilt in 1955 and its gilding renewed in 1987. The pond garden with its islands and rocks dates largely from Yoshimitsu's time. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

title: Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
creator: zen-temple-builders
note: Ashikaga Yoshimasa's retreat in the eastern hills, where the shoin room of later Japanese houses took shape.
description: The shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, having retired amid the devastation of the Ōnin War, began a villa at the foot of the eastern hills of Kyoto in 1482, modelled on Saihō-ji and his grandfather's Golden Pavilion. It became the Zen temple Jishō-ji after his death in 1490. The two-storey Kannon Hall, completed in 1489, was never covered in silver, despite its popular name; its lower floor is in residential style and its upper floor in the Zen style. The nearby Tōgu-dō, of 1486, contains the Dōjinsai, a small study of four and a half mats with a built-in desk and staggered shelves, the oldest surviving example of the shoin room that became the basis of the formal Japanese interior. Yoshimasa's circle at the villa made it a centre of Higashiyama culture: tea, ink painting, flower arrangement and Noh. The raked sand terrace and cone in the garden were added in the Edo period.

title: Rock Garden of Ryōan-ji
creator: zen-temple-builders
note: Fifteen stones on raked white gravel, the most famous dry landscape garden in Japan.
description: Ryōan-ji was founded in 1450 by the warrior Hosokawa Katsumoto and rebuilt after the Ōnin War in 1499. In front of its abbot's quarters lies a rectangular courtyard enclosed on two sides by an earthen wall, in which fifteen stones, set in five groups with moss at their bases, rest on a bed of white gravel raked in lines. From any point on the viewing veranda at least one stone is hidden. The garden's date, designer and meaning are unknown. It is often attributed to the painter Sōami, but this is not documented, and the names of two workmen are carved on one stone; scholars have proposed dates from the late fifteenth to the seventeenth century. Interpretations range from islands in the sea to a tigress with cubs. Little noticed before the twentieth century, it became a modern emblem of Zen and of abstract composition. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

title: Daisen-in
creator: zen-temple-builders
note: A tiny dry landscape garden that depicts a river flowing from mountains to the sea.
description: Daisen-in, a subtemple of the great Zen monastery of Daitoku-ji, was founded in 1509 by the monk Kogaku Sōkō, and its abbot's quarters, of 1513, are among the oldest surviving buildings of their type. The narrow garden wrapped around the building's north-east corner is a celebrated dry landscape: tall upright stones and clipped shrubs represent mountains and a waterfall, white gravel a river that flows under a stone bridge and past a stone 'treasure ship', widening into a sea of raked gravel on the south side. Its compression of a whole landscape into a few square metres recalls Chinese ink landscape painting. The designer is unknown, though the garden is sometimes attributed to Kogaku Sōkō himself or to Sōami. The main hall is a National Treasure.

title: Himeji Castle
creator: japanese-castle-builders
note: The 'White Heron Castle', the finest surviving Japanese castle with its original keep.
description: A fort on Himeyama hill was enlarged by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 1580s, and after the battle of Sekigahara Tokugawa Ieyasu's son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa rebuilt it on a grand scale between 1601 and 1609. The main keep rises from a high battered stone base to five roofs outside, with six floors and a basement inside, linked by corridors to three smaller keeps. Its walls are coated in white plaster for fire resistance, and its gables and layered roofs give it a soaring, bird-like appearance. A spiralling maze of gates, baileys and walls, with loopholes for guns and arrows and openings for dropping stones, protected the approach. Of the castle's buildings, more than eighty survive. It escaped the demolitions of the Meiji period and the bombing of 1945, and was restored in the 1950s and again from 2009 to 2015. In 1993 it became one of Japan's first World Heritage Sites.

title: Matsumoto Castle
creator: japanese-castle-builders
note: A black-walled castle on the plain, among the oldest original keeps in Japan.
description: Matsumoto Castle was built on the flat land of the Matsumoto basin rather than on a hill, and so relies on a wide moat for defence. Its main keep and attached smaller keep are usually dated to the 1590s, when the domain was held by Ishikawa Kazumasa and his son Yasunaga, though the exact date is debated. Its walls are clad in black lacquered boards, which earned it the nickname 'Crow Castle'. In the more peaceful 1630s a turret for moon-viewing with an open veranda was added, a contrast between military and leisure architecture. After the Meiji Restoration the castle was sold for demolition, but local citizens bought it back, and it was later restored. Its keep is one of five designated National Treasures.

title: Nijō Castle
creator: nakai-masakiyo
note: The Kyoto residence of the Tokugawa shōguns, with the painted audience halls of the Ninomaru Palace.
description: Tokugawa Ieyasu built Nijō Castle as his residence in the imperial capital, with Nakai Masakiyo as master carpenter, completing it in 1603, the year he became shōgun. It was enlarged in 1624–26 for the visit of Emperor Go-Mizunoo, when Kobori Enshū was among those working on the gardens. The Ninomaru Palace that survives is a sequence of halls connected diagonally, in the shoin style, whose rooms rise in rank towards the shōgun's audience chamber; their walls and sliding doors are painted by the Kanō school with pines, tigers and flowers on gold ground, and the corridors have 'nightingale floors' that squeak underfoot. The castle's keep burned in 1750. In 1867 the last shōgun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, announced the return of power to the emperor there. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

title: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
creator: kora-munehiro
note: The lavishly carved and gilded mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, centred on the Yōmeimon gate.
description: Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate, was deified after his death in 1616 as Tōshō Daigongen, and a shrine was built for him at Nikkō in the mountains north of Edo in 1617. His grandson Iemitsu had it rebuilt on a far grander scale in 1634–36, under the master carpenter Kōra Munehiro. The main shrine follows the gongen-zukuri plan, in which a worship hall and the main sanctuary are joined by a linking room under a complex roof. Every surface of the buildings is lacquered, gilded or carved with dragons, birds, flowers and figures from Chinese legend, among them the famous three monkeys and the sleeping cat; the Yōmeimon gate alone carries more than five hundred carvings. The shrine is set among tall cryptomeria trees approached by stairs. It is part of the Shrines and Temples of Nikkō World Heritage Site.

title: Tai-an tea room
creator: sen-no-rikyu
note: A two-mat tea room traditionally attributed to Sen no Rikyū, the archetype of the wabi tea house.
description: The Tai-an, at the Zen temple Myōki-an in Yamazaki south-west of Kyoto, is traditionally said to have been built by Sen no Rikyū around 1582, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi had a base at Yamazaki after defeating Akechi Mitsuhide. It may have been moved to its present site. The room has just two tatami mats for host and guests, with a small alcove (tokonoma) whose corners and ceiling are plastered over to make it seem deeper, walls of rough clay mixed with straw, small windows of paper and lattice and a low ceiling of different heights. Guests enter by crawling through a small square opening, the nijiriguchi, leaving rank and swords outside. It is the oldest surviving tea house in Japan and a National Treasure, and can be visited only by advance appointment. It embodies Rikyū's ideal of tea in a space of humility and concentration.

title: Katsura Imperial Villa
creator: prince-toshihito
note: The princely villa on the Katsura River, the classic synthesis of sukiya architecture and garden.
description: Prince Hachijō Toshihito began the villa around 1615 on land associated with the Tale of Genji, and his son Prince Toshitada enlarged it from the 1640s, so that the main building is a staggered line of three shoin linked diagonally: the Old Shoin with its bamboo moon-viewing platform, the Middle Shoin and the New Palace. Around a pond with islands, a stroll garden leads past tea houses such as the Shōkintei, each revealing a new view. The buildings combine the formal shoin style with the rustic materials and asymmetry of the tea house: unpainted wood, paper screens, tatami and refined but simple details. The design was long credited to Kobori Enshū, but this is now considered a legend. In 1933 the German architect Bruno Taut praised it as a model of functional modern design, and Walter Gropius and Kenzō Tange later wrote on it. It is administered by the Imperial Household Agency and can be visited by reservation.

title: Crane and Turtle Garden of Konchi-in
creator: kobori-enshu
note: A dry garden of crane and turtle islands designed by Kobori Enshū for the abbot Ishin Sūden.
description: Konchi-in is a subtemple of Nanzen-ji, moved to its present site in 1605 by the abbot Ishin Sūden, a powerful adviser to Tokugawa Ieyasu who also enshrined Ieyasu there in a small Tōshō-gū. Around 1632 Kobori Enshū designed the garden in front of the abbot's quarters, one of the few gardens firmly documented as his, built by the gardener Kentei. A broad expanse of white gravel stands for the sea; on either side, stones and clipped shrubs form a crane island and a turtle island, symbols of longevity, framing a large flat worship stone at the centre, with a hillside of trees behind. The temple also contains the Hassō-seki tea room, attributed to Enshū. The garden shows his combination of bold, clear composition with the auspicious imagery favoured by the Tokugawa.

title: Gasshō Houses of Shirakawa-gō
creator: vernacular-builders
note: Steep thatched farmhouses of the Japanese Alps, built for heavy snow and silkworm raising.
description: In the isolated mountain valleys of Shirakawa-gō and Gokayama, farmers built large houses in the gasshō-zukuri style, named after the resemblance of their steep roofs to hands joined in prayer. The thatched roofs, at about sixty degrees, shed the heavy snow of the region, and the large attic spaces under them, on several floors, were used for raising silkworms and producing saltpetre. Extended families lived on the ground floor around an open hearth, whose smoke preserved the thatch and timbers. The roofs are rethatched every few decades by the villagers working together in a tradition of mutual help called yui. Ogimachi in Shirakawa-gō preserves the largest group, and the villages were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1995.

title: Rokumeikan
creator: conder
note: The Western-style hall where the Meiji elite held balls for foreign diplomats.
description: The Rokumeikan, the 'Deer-Cry Pavilion', was commissioned by the foreign minister Inoue Kaoru as a place where Japanese officials could entertain foreign diplomats in Western style, as part of an effort to persuade the Western powers to revise the unequal treaties. Designed by Josiah Conder and opened in 1883, it was a two-storey building of brick and stucco with arcaded verandas, combining French Second Empire and Italianate features with Indo-Saracenic touches. Balls, concerts and bazaars were held there, and the 'Rokumeikan era' became a byword for superficial Westernisation, mocked by critics and cartoonists. After the policy changed the building became a club for the peerage. It was demolished in 1940.

title: Former Iwasaki Residence
creator: conder
note: Conder's wooden Western mansion for the head of Mitsubishi, joined to a Japanese wing.
description: In 1896 Josiah Conder completed a mansion for Iwasaki Hisaya, the third head of the Mitsubishi company, on an estate near Ueno. The main house, built of timber, is in a Jacobean manner with a two-storey veranda of colonnades towards the garden and richly carved interiors, and a separate billiard room is built like a Swiss chalet. A large Japanese-style residence was attached, of which only a part survives. The combination of Western reception rooms and Japanese living quarters was typical of Meiji elite houses. The surviving buildings are Important Cultural Properties, and the house and garden are open to the public as the Kyū-Iwasaki-tei Garden.
image_file: Kyu Iwasaki tei in Taitō-ku,Tokyo - Entrance Hall.jpg
image_caption: Entrance hall of the Former Iwasaki Residence

title: Bank of Japan Head Office
creator: tatsuno-kingo
note: The first major Western-style building designed by a Japanese architect, in stone.
description: The Bank of Japan was founded in 1882, and Tatsuno Kingo, after studying central bank buildings in Europe, designed its head office in Nihonbashi, completed in 1896. It is a building of brick faced with granite and andesite, in a restrained Neo-Baroque manner, arranged around a courtyard and entered through a gateway, with a central dome. Its design was adapted for the risk of earthquakes, and the upper floors were partly lightened after the Nōbi earthquake of 1891 during construction. It survived the Kantō earthquake of 1923 and the war. The building, still part of the bank, is an Important Cultural Property and houses the Bank of Japan's currency museum nearby.
image_caption: Bank of Japan head office, Tokyo

title: Tokyo Station
creator: tatsuno-kingo
note: Tatsuno's long red-brick station building facing the Imperial Palace.
description: Tokyo Station opened in 1914 as the central terminus of Japan's railways, facing the Imperial Palace across the Marunouchi business district. Tatsuno Kingo's Marunouchi building is about 335 metres long, of red brick with bands of white stone, with domed halls at the north and south ends and a central entrance reserved for the imperial family. Its steel frame helped it survive the Kantō earthquake of 1923. In the air raids of 1945 the roof and domes burned, and the building was repaired with only two storeys and simplified roofs. A major restoration completed in 2012 rebuilt the third storey and the domes to the original design and added seismic isolation beneath the building. It is an Important Cultural Property.

title: Akasaka Palace
creator: katayama-tokuma
note: A neo-Baroque palace built for the crown prince, now the State Guest House of Japan.
description: The Tōgū Palace was built between 1899 and 1909 as the residence of the crown prince, the future Emperor Taishō. Katayama Tōkuma, architect of the Imperial Household, modelled it on European palaces, with a symmetrical facade of granite, a central entrance and curving wings, and lavish interiors decorated by Japanese and European craftsmen, including panels of cloisonné and paintings by leading artists. Its steel frame and brick walls were designed with earthquakes in mind. It was little used as a residence, and after the Second World War served as the National Diet Library and other offices. Renovated by Murano Tōgo and others, it became the State Guest House in 1974 for visiting heads of state. In 2009 it was designated a National Treasure, the first building of the Meiji era or later to be so honoured.

title: Imperial Hotel
creator: wright
location: Uchisaiwaichō, Tokyo, Japan; entrance now at Meiji Mura, Inuyama
note: Frank Lloyd Wright's Tokyo hotel of brick and carved stone, which survived the Great Kantō earthquake.
description: The Imperial Hotel, Japan's main hotel for foreign guests, commissioned Frank Lloyd Wright in 1916 to design a new building. Construction, delayed by costs and a fire, ran from 1919 to 1923, and Wright left before it was complete, with his Japanese assistant Endō Arata finishing it. The hotel had an H-shaped plan of low wings around courts and pools, built of reinforced concrete and brick faced with yellow tapestry brick and carved Ōya stone, a soft volcanic tuff, with intricate geometrical ornament. Wright designed its foundations to 'float' on the mud and cantilevered its floors to resist earthquakes. It came through the Great Kantō earthquake of 1 September 1923, the day of its formal opening, with little damage, a story Wright made famous. The building was demolished in 1968 despite protests, and its entrance hall and lobby were reconstructed at the Meiji Mura open-air museum in Inuyama.
image_file: Main Entrance Hall and Lobby, Imperial Hotel in Meiji Mura 2022.jpg
image_caption: Entrance hall and lobby of the Imperial Hotel, reconstructed at Meiji Mura, Inuyama

title: Jiyū Gakuen Myōnichikan
creator: wright
note: A low Prairie-style school building designed by Wright for a progressive girls' school.
description: Hani Motoko and her husband Yoshikazu, journalists and educational reformers, founded the Jiyū Gakuen ('School of Freedom') for girls in 1921, and asked Frank Lloyd Wright, then in Tokyo for the Imperial Hotel, to design the building, with Endō Arata. The Myōnichikan, the 'House of Tomorrow', is a symmetrical, low timber and stucco building in the manner of Wright's Prairie houses, with a central hall lit by tall geometrical windows and two wings of classrooms embracing a lawn. After the school moved, the building was used by its alumnae. It was designated an Important Cultural Property in 1997 and restored, and is open to visitors and used for events.

title: St Paul's Catholic Church, Karuizawa
creator: antonin-raymond
note: A timber church with a steep roof and exposed frame, Raymond's fusion of modernism and craft.
description: Karuizawa, a summer resort in the mountains favoured by missionaries and foreigners, was where Antonin Raymond built this small Catholic church in 1935. It has a tall, steep roof and a pointed bell tower, with walls of rough timber and an interior of exposed scissor trusses and diagonal bracing in unpainted wood, made by Japanese carpenters. Raymond acknowledged that the design was inspired by an unbuilt house project by Le Corbusier, the Errázuriz House for Chile, and adapted it to Japanese building craft. The result combines the forms of Central European rural churches with Japanese carpentry and has become a much-loved place for weddings. It was later celebrated as an early example of a regional modern architecture in Japan.
image_file: St. Paul's Catholic Church Karuizawa Japan 2010.jpg

title: Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura
creator: sakakura
location: Tsurugaoka Hachimangū, Kamakura, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan
note: Japan's first public museum of modern art, a white box raised over a lotus pond.
description: Junzō Sakakura designed the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura, opened in 1951 in the grounds of the Tsurugaoka Hachimangū shrine, as a small, inexpensive building in the difficult years after the war. A two-storey box clad in white panels encloses a courtyard, and part of it is raised on slender steel columns over the Heike pond, so that reflected light plays on its underside. Open-air terraces and a stair lead from the courtyard to the galleries. The building applied lessons from Le Corbusier's museum projects to a Japanese site with remarkable delicacy. The museum moved out in 2016 when its lease ended; the shrine preserved the building, which reopened in 2019 as the Kamakura Bunkakan Tsurugaoka Museum.
image_file: The Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura 2009.jpg

title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and Park
creator: tange
note: Tange's memorial ensemble on the site of the atomic bombing, aligned on the ruined Genbaku Dome.
description: In 1949 Kenzō Tange won the competition for a peace park on the delta island at the centre of the atomic explosion of 6 August 1945. He drew a single axis from the main museum building, through a saddle-shaped cenotaph inspired by ancient clay house models, to the ruined dome of the former Industrial Promotion Hall, now the Genbaku Dome. The museum, completed in 1955, is a long concrete building raised on pilotis, with a facade of vertical louvres, through which the axis passes unobstructed. The design combined Le Corbusier's modernism with the proportions of traditional timber architecture. The main building was designated an Important Cultural Property in 2006, the first postwar buildings to be so designated, and the Genbaku Dome became a World Heritage Site in 1996.

title: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
creator: tange
note: Two cable-suspended arenas built for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, a landmark of structural expression.
description: For the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the first held in Asia, Kenzō Tange and the structural engineer Yoshikatsu Tsuboi designed two arenas in Yoyogi Park. In the larger, built for swimming and diving, two main steel cables are slung between two concrete masts and anchored to the ground, and the roof is suspended from them on secondary cables, producing sweeping curves that recall both the roofs of temples and the forms of shells. The smaller arena, for basketball, has a spiralling roof hung from a single mast. The arenas were built in about eighteen months and impressed the world as a sign of Japan's postwar recovery. They have remained in use for sports and concerts, and were designated an Important Cultural Property in 2021.

title: St Mary's Cathedral, Tokyo
creator: tange
note: The Catholic cathedral of Tokyo, eight shells of stainless steel that rise into a cross of light.
description: The Catholic cathedral of Tokyo, a timber Gothic building, was destroyed in an air raid in 1945. For the new cathedral, completed in 1964, Kenzō Tange and Yoshikatsu Tsuboi designed eight hyperbolic paraboloid concrete shells that lean together and rise from a diamond-shaped plan to a height of about 40 metres. Between the shells narrow skylights form a cross that runs the length of the roof and down the facades, bringing light into the tall, unadorned concrete interior. The exterior is clad in stainless steel. A separate bell tower stands about 60 metres high. The cathedral is one of the most admired works of Tange's mature period.
image_file: 20030702 2 July 2003 Tokyo Cathedorale 1 Tange Kenzou Sekiguchi Tokyo Japan b.jpg

title: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
creator: tange
note: The twin-towered city hall of Tokyo, Tange's late monument in Shinjuku.
description: When the Tokyo metropolitan government moved its headquarters from Marunouchi to the new skyscraper district of Shinjuku, Kenzō Tange won the competition with a design completed in 1991. The main building is 243 metres high and divides at its 33rd floor into two towers, an outline often compared to a Gothic cathedral, and is accompanied by a second tower and an assembly building around a semicircular plaza. The granite and glass facades carry a fine grid pattern that has been compared both to traditional lattice and to the circuits of a computer chip. It was the tallest building in Tokyo until 2007, and its free observation decks are among the city's most visited viewpoints.

title: Sky House
creator: kikutake
note: Kikutake's own house, a single room on four concrete panels, a founding work of Metabolism.
description: Kiyonori Kikutake built the Sky House for himself and his wife, the poet Norie Kikutake, on a slope in Tokyo in 1958. A single square room of about ten metres a side, under a hyperbolic paraboloid concrete roof, is lifted high above the ground on four wall-like piers set at the midpoint of each side. Around its edge the kitchen, bathroom and storage were designed as 'move-net' units that could be replaced as needs changed, and a children's room was later hung beneath the floor. The house thus expressed in miniature the Metabolist idea of a permanent structure supporting changeable parts, two years before the group's manifesto. It has been altered over time and is still a private house.

title: Edo-Tokyo Museum
creator: kikutake
note: A museum of the city's history lifted high on four giant legs, a late work of Metabolism.
description: Kiyonori Kikutake's museum of the history of Edo and Tokyo opened in 1993 near the Ryōgoku sumo arena. Its main exhibition floors are raised on four enormous concrete legs, leaving a large open plaza beneath, and the building's height of about 62 metres was set to match that of the long-vanished keep of Edo Castle. The form is said to evoke a traditional raised storehouse. Inside, full-size reconstructions include half of the Nihonbashi bridge and a kabuki theatre facade. The museum's massive scale divided critics, but it became a familiar Tokyo landmark. It closed for a long renovation in 2022.

title: Nakagin Capsule Tower
creator: kurokawa
note: Kurokawa's tower of prefabricated capsules, the most famous built work of Metabolism.
description: Kishō Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower, completed in 1972 in Ginza, consisted of 140 prefabricated steel capsules, each a tiny studio of about 10 square metres with a built-in bed, bathroom unit and a round window, attached to two concrete cores of eleven and thirteen storeys. The capsules were factory-made, delivered by truck and bolted to the cores, and were intended as pieds-à-terre for businessmen. In principle they could be replaced every few decades, the Metabolist ideal of a building that renews itself, but none ever was. The building decayed, and despite international campaigns for its preservation it was demolished in 2022. Some capsules were salvaged and restored for museums and other uses.

title: National Art Center, Tokyo
creator: kurokawa
note: Kurokawa's last major building, with an undulating glass facade, one of Japan's largest exhibition spaces.
description: The National Art Center opened in Roppongi in 2007, shortly before Kishō Kurokawa's death, as a venue for temporary exhibitions without a permanent collection. Its main facade is a wall of glass louvres that ripples in a wave along the front of the building, filtering sunlight into a vast atrium. Inside the atrium two inverted concrete cones rise from the floor, carrying a restaurant and café at their tops. Behind lie twelve large exhibition rooms. The building embodies Kurokawa's late idea of symbiosis between architecture and nature, and has become one of the most visited art venues in Japan.
image_file: The National Art Center , Tokyo - panoramio (1).jpg

title: Hillside Terrace
creator: maki
note: A street of low buildings designed over twenty-three years, a model of gradual urban design.
description: In 1967 the Asakura family, landowners in Daikanyama, asked Fumihiko Maki to design housing and shops on their property along the Kyū-Yamate Avenue. He built the complex in six phases between 1969 and 1992, adapting each to new needs, materials and regulations while keeping a consistent low scale, small courtyards, setbacks, passages and public spaces that open the buildings to the street. The early phases are in white concrete, the later ones in metal and glass. The result is a piece of city rather than a single object, an application of Maki's idea of 'group form'. Hillside Terrace helped turn Daikanyama into one of Tokyo's most pleasant neighbourhoods and is often cited as a model of patient, collaborative development.

title: Spiral
creator: maki
note: Maki's collage-like building for the lingerie company Wacoal, with a spiralling ramp inside.
description: Spiral was built in 1985 for the Wacoal company as a cultural complex on Aoyama-dōri, with a gallery, hall, shops and restaurant. Its street facade is a carefully composed collage of grids, a cone, a cube and fragments of aluminium and glass that mirror the variety of the surrounding city. Inside, a spiralling ramp curves up around the edge of a semicircular top-lit gallery behind the entrance, giving the building its name. It is often seen as one of the best works of 1980s Tokyo, showing how a small urban building can create a public interior.

title: Museum of Modern Art, Gunma
creator: isozaki
note: Isozaki's museum built as an assembly of cubes, a step from Metabolism towards postmodernism.
description: The Gunma Prefectural Museum of Modern Art, opened in 1974 in a park at Takasaki, was designed by Arata Isozaki as a framework of cubes of about twelve metres a side, defining a geometric grid against which the galleries are arranged. The cubes are clad in square aluminium panels and glass, and a separate wing for Japanese art is set at an angle, projecting over a pool. Isozaki described the cube as a neutral 'framework' for art, rejecting the expressive forms of his elders. Together with his writings of the period, the building marked his turn to an architecture of pure geometry, ideas and quotation.
image_file: 261010 The Museum of Modern Art, Gunma Takasaki Japan03s3.jpg

title: Tsukuba Center Building
creator: isozaki
type: Civic centre with hotel and concert hall
note: A landmark of postmodern architecture, built around a sunken plaza quoting Michelangelo.
description: Tsukuba Science City was built by the Japanese state from the 1960s as a new town of research institutes. Its centre, designed by Arata Isozaki and completed in 1983, contains a hotel, concert hall, information centre and shops around a sunken oval plaza. The plaza is an inverted copy of Michelangelo's Piazza del Campidoglio in Rome, and the buildings quote Ledoux, Michael Graves and other sources, with rusticated stone, metal and tile. Isozaki said that a city of bureaucratic planning had no real centre, and that his quotation of Western forms around an empty space expressed this absence. The building became one of the most discussed examples of postmodernism.

title: Row House in Sumiyoshi (Azuma House)
creator: ando
note: A tiny concrete house split by an open courtyard, the work that made Tadao Andō's name.
description: In a dense neighbourhood of old wooden row houses in Osaka, Tadao Andō replaced one narrow house with a closed box of exposed concrete, about 3.6 metres wide and 14 metres deep, with no windows to the street and only a single doorway. The interior is divided into three equal parts, of which the central one is an open courtyard; to go from the living room to the kitchen or the bedroom, the occupants must pass through the open air, even in rain. Andō argued that this restored contact with nature and the seasons in the city. The house won the Architectural Institute of Japan prize in 1979 and established his reputation and his language of concrete, light and geometry.

title: Church of the Light
creator: ando
note: A concrete chapel in which a cross of light is cut into the wall behind the altar.
description: The Ibaraki Kasugaoka Church, a small Protestant congregation in a suburb of Osaka, had a very limited budget for its new chapel, completed in 1989. Tadao Andō designed a concrete box crossed at an angle by a freestanding wall that defines the entrance. Behind the altar the end wall is cut by a cruciform opening from floor to ceiling, so that the cross is made of daylight; the floor and pews are of rough-sawn timber and descend towards it. Andō had wanted the openings left unglazed, but glass was installed. A Sunday school building was added in 1999. The chapel has become one of the most famous religious buildings of the late twentieth century.
image_caption: Cross of light, Church of the Light

title: Chichu Art Museum
creator: ando
note: A museum built almost entirely underground on an island in the Inland Sea, lit by daylight.
description: The Chichu Art Museum was built in 2004 for the Benesse foundation on Naoshima, an island that has become a centre of contemporary art. To preserve the landscape of a former salt field, Tadao Andō placed the museum underground, revealing only geometric openings, courtyards and slots in the hillside. It houses permanent installations of a few artists: late Water Lilies by Claude Monet in a white room lit from above, a large work by Walter De Maria and light installations by James Turrell. The rooms are lit mainly by natural daylight, so that the experience of the art changes with the time of day and the season. It is one of several buildings by Andō on the island.
image_file: 150505 Chichu Art Museum Naoshima Island Kagawa pref Japan01s3.jpg

title: Sendai Mediatheque
creator: toyo-ito
location: Kasugamachi, Aoba, Sendai, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan
note: A glass cube whose floors are held up by thirteen tree-like tubes of steel lattice.
description: Toyo Itō won the competition for a library, gallery and media centre in Sendai in 1995, and the building opened in 2001. It is a cube of glass about 50 metres square, with seven thin floor plates of steel honeycomb supported by thirteen hollow tubes of welded steel pipes that rise through the building at irregular positions, swaying like seaweed in water. The tubes contain stairs, lifts and services and bring daylight down through the floors. The building has no conventional walls inside, and each floor has a different layout and furniture. It survived the strong shaking of the 2011 earthquake with damage mostly to ceilings, and is regarded as one of the defining buildings of its decade.

title: Tama Art University Library
creator: toyo-ito
note: A library of thin concrete arches of varying spans, set into a sloping site.
description: For the library of the Tama Art University campus at Hachiōji, completed in 2007, Toyo Itō designed a structure of thin arches of concrete with a steel core, arranged along curving lines that cross one another at irregular intervals, so that the arches have different spans and the spaces between them shift continuously. The ground floor follows the natural slope of the site, rising as a gentle incline. The glazed facades are flush with the arches, so that the building looks like a light, cave-like grid. The open, flowing interior is used both as a library and a common space for students, and the building is often cited as a key work of Itō's structural experiments.

title: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa
creator: sanaa
note: A low glass disc containing scattered white galleries, open from every side.
description: The 21st Century Museum in Kanazawa, opened in 2004, was designed by Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa as a single-storey disc about 112 metres in diameter, enclosed by glass walls and entered from four sides, so that it has no front or back and invites people in from the surrounding park and city. Within the disc, galleries of different sizes and heights are scattered like boxes, separated by corridors and light courts, with free public areas in between. The best-known artwork, Leandro Erlich's swimming pool, lets visitors appear to stand under water. The building won the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale of 2004 and helped make SANAA internationally famous.
image_file: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa011.jpg
image_caption: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa

title: Teshima Art Museum
creator: sanaa
note: Ryue Nishizawa's concrete shell open to the sky, housing a single work by Rei Naitō.
description: On a hillside among rice terraces on the island of Teshima in the Inland Sea, Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naitō created in 2010 a museum for a single work. The building is a thin, low concrete shell about 40 by 60 metres and only about 4.5 metres high at its highest point, with no columns, shaped like a drop of water. It was made by pouring concrete over a carefully shaped mound of earth, which was then dug out. Two large oval openings let in light, wind, rain and the sound of birds. On the floor, tiny springs release droplets of water that gather and flow across the surface in Naitō's work Matrix. Visitors are asked to remove their shoes and be silent. It is part of the Setouchi art islands project.

title: Japan National Stadium
creator: kuma
note: Kengo Kuma's stadium for the Tokyo Olympics, with layered eaves of Japanese cedar.
description: The stadium for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics was first to be built to a design by Zaha Hadid, but the government cancelled it in 2015 because of its cost. A new competition was won by a team of Kengo Kuma with the construction company Taisei. The stadium, completed in 2019 on the site of the 1958 National Stadium, is lower and flatter than Hadid's design, with tiers of eaves faced with timber louvres of cedar and larch from all of Japan's forty-seven prefectures, planting along the terraces and a roof of steel and timber. It held the opening and closing ceremonies of the Olympics, postponed to 2021 because of the pandemic and held without spectators.
image_file: Japan National Stadium C-gate on 2021 July 28.jpg

title: Nezu Museum
creator: kuma
note: A museum of Asian art with a great sheltering tiled roof and a bamboo-lined approach.
description: The Nezu Museum holds the collection of Japanese and East Asian art formed by the businessman Nezu Kaichirō, including famous screens by Ogata Kōrin. Its new building by Kengo Kuma, opened in 2009, presents to the busy avenue of Aoyama a long approach under bamboo, then a low building dominated by a large pitched roof of dark tiles with deep eaves, supported on thin steel. Inside, glass walls look out over the museum's large garden of ponds, tea houses and stone lanterns. The building was praised for its calm and its relation to the garden, and is one of Kuma's best-known works in Tokyo.

title: Cardboard Cathedral
creator: shigeru-ban
note: A transitional cathedral of cardboard tubes built after the Christchurch earthquake.
description: The Christchurch earthquake of February 2011 badly damaged the city's Anglican cathedral, and Shigeru Ban offered to design a transitional cathedral, opened in 2013. Its triangular A-frame is formed of large cardboard tubes, coated against water and fire and stiffened by timber, rising from a base of shipping containers that house side rooms, under a roof of polycarbonate. The triangular front is filled with coloured glass with images from the earlier cathedral's rose window. Seating some 700 people, it serves as a church and concert venue. It was intended to last some decades while the permanent cathedral is restored, and became a symbol of the city's recovery.

title: Ōita Prefectural Art Museum
creator: shigeru-ban
note: A museum whose glass walls fold away to open the atrium to the street.
description: The Ōita Prefectural Art Museum, opened in 2015 in the centre of Ōita, was designed by Shigeru Ban to be a 'living room' for the city. Along the main street, the ground-floor facade is made of tall glass panels that can be folded away like sliding doors, so that the atrium, used for events and free exhibitions, merges with the pavement. The upper floor is wrapped in a lattice of timber and steel inspired by traditional bamboo craft, a local industry, and the interior uses timber structures that Ban has explored throughout his career. The building is an example of his ideal of an open, flexible public architecture.

title: Tokyo Bunka Kaikan
creator: maekawa
note: Maekawa's concert hall in Ueno Park, facing the museum built by his teacher Le Corbusier.
description: The Tokyo Bunka Kaikan, opened in 1961 to mark the 500th anniversary of the founding of Edo, was Tokyo's main hall for opera, ballet and orchestral music for decades. Kunio Maekawa placed it in Ueno Park opposite the National Museum of Western Art, completed in 1959 to a design by Le Corbusier, for whom Maekawa had worked in Paris. A massive concrete roof with a deep upturned edge, like the eaves of a temple, shelters the foyers and the main hall of over 2,000 seats, whose walls are lined with sculptural acoustic panels. The building is a key example of the heroic concrete modernism of postwar Japan, and has been renovated several times.

title: Goguryeo Tombs
creator: three-kingdoms-korean-builders
location: Pyongyang and Nampo region, North Korea; Ji'an, Jilin, China
note: Stone-chambered tombs of the Goguryeo kingdom, many painted with murals of daily life and the cosmos.
description: Goguryeo, the northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, ruled a territory spanning present-day northern Korea and north-east China until 668. Its kings and nobles were buried in tombs of two main types: stepped pyramids of cut stone, such as the so-called General's Tomb near Ji'an, and earth mounds over stone chambers. Many chambers have corbelled 'lantern' ceilings and walls painted with hunting scenes, processions, houses, stars and the guardian animals of the four directions, which are valuable evidence for the lost timber architecture of the period. The tomb attributed to King Dongmyeong, the kingdom's legendary founder, near Pyongyang was heavily restored in the 1990s. The tombs in North Korea and in China were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2004.
image_caption: Tomb attributed to King Tongmyong (Dongmyeong), near Pyongyang

title: Stone Pagoda of Mireuksa
creator: three-kingdoms-korean-builders
location: Iksan, North Jeolla Province, South Korea
note: The oldest and largest surviving Korean stone pagoda, built by the Baekje kingdom.
description: Mireuksa was the largest Buddhist temple of the Baekje kingdom, founded by King Mu in the early seventh century with three precincts, each with a pagoda and hall, dedicated to the future Buddha Maitreya. The western pagoda, of granite, imitates the forms of a timber pagoda, with corner posts, beams and flaring eaves cut in stone. A reliquary found during restoration in 2009, with an inscription dated 639, revealed that it was commissioned by a Baekje queen. By modern times only six storeys of one side survived, propped up with concrete by Japanese restorers in 1915. After a dismantling and reconstruction lasting from 2001 to 2018, it again stands about 14.5 metres high. It is part of the Baekje Historic Areas World Heritage Site.

title: Five-storey Stone Pagoda of Jeongnimsa
creator: three-kingdoms-korean-builders
location: Buyeo, South Chungcheong Province, South Korea
note: An elegant Baekje stone pagoda in the last Baekje capital, Sabi.
description: Jeongnimsa was the central temple of Sabi (present-day Buyeo), the last capital of Baekje from 538 to 660. Its five-storey granite pagoda, about 8.3 metres high, has slender proportions and thin, broad eaves that turn up slightly at the corners, a refined translation of timber forms into stone. When the Tang and Silla armies conquered Baekje in 660, the Tang general carved a victory inscription on its base, which led to its being misnamed for centuries as a Tang monument. It is one of only two surviving Baekje pagodas, with that of Mireuksa, and is part of the Baekje Historic Areas World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Five-storey stone pagoda and site of Jeongnimsa

title: Nine-storey Pagoda of Hwangnyongsa
creator: abiji
location: Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: A wooden pagoda about eighty metres tall, built by a Baekje master for Silla's royal temple.
description: Hwangnyongsa, the 'Temple of the Yellow Dragon', was founded in 553 by King Jinheung of Silla as the kingdom's main royal temple. In the 640s Queen Seondeok, on the advice of the monk Jajang, ordered a nine-storey wooden pagoda to protect the realm, and according to the Samguk yusa the Baekje master builder Abiji raised it, completing it in 645. Its height is recorded as about 80 metres, which would have made it the tallest structure in East Asia. It was repaired several times and burned with the whole temple during the Mongol invasion of 1238. Excavations from 1976 uncovered the foundation stones of the pagoda and halls, and the temple's plan and a scale model of the pagoda can be seen at a museum on the site, which is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas World Heritage Site.
image_file: A scale model of Hwangnyongsa pagoda.jpg
image_caption: Scale model of the nine-storey pagoda of Hwangnyongsa

title: Cheomseongdae
creator: silla-builders
location: Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: A bottle-shaped stone tower of Silla, the oldest surviving observatory structure in East Asia.
description: Cheomseongdae stands in the old Silla capital Gyeongju and is traditionally dated to the reign of Queen Seondeok (632–647). It is a tower about 9 metres high made of 27 courses of curved granite blocks forming a bottle-like profile, topped by a square frame of long stones, with a square opening halfway up. Its use has been debated: the usual view is that it was an astronomical observatory, but some scholars have seen it as a symbolic monument relating to the calendar or Buddhist cosmology, or as a ritual altar. Numerological readings of the numbers of stones and courses are popular but uncertain. It is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas World Heritage Site.
image_file: Cheomseongdae Observatory under blue sky in Gyeongju South Korea.jpg

title: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond
creator: silla-builders
location: Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: The pond garden of the Silla crown prince's palace, long known as Anapji.
description: After the unification of the Korean peninsula under Silla, King Munmu created in 674 a pond with islands and hills in the grounds of the palace of the crown prince, where banquets were held for envoys and court. The pond, with irregular shores designed so that its full extent can never be seen from one point, was planted with flowers and stocked with rare birds and animals. The palace fell into ruin and the pond was later called Anapji, 'pond of geese and ducks'. Dredging in the 1970s recovered tens of thousands of objects, including roof tiles, a wooden game die and the remains of a boat, and several pavilions were reconstructed on their original foundations. It is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas World Heritage Site.

image_caption: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond, Gyeongju

title: Bulguksa
creator: kim-dae-seong
location: Mount Toham, Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: Silla's great temple on its stone terraces, with the twin pagodas Dabotap and Seokgatap.
description: Bulguksa, the 'Temple of the Buddha Land', was enlarged from a smaller temple from 751, according to tradition by the minister Kim Dae-seong, and completed by the state after his death in 774. It stands on great stone terraces approached by two pairs of stone stairways treated as bridges, the Blue Cloud and White Cloud Bridges and the Lotus Flower and Seven Treasures Bridges, symbolising passage from the world into the Buddha's realm. In the courtyard before the main hall stand two contrasting stone pagodas: the austere Seokgatap and the intricate Dabotap, which translates a complex timber structure into stone. In 1966 a printed dharani sutra, one of the oldest printed texts in the world, was found inside Seokgatap. The timber halls were burned during the Japanese invasions of 1592 and rebuilt; the temple was extensively restored in 1969–73. With Seokguram it became a World Heritage Site in 1995.
image_file: Lotus Flower Bridge and Seven Treasure Bridge at Bulguksa in Gyeongju, Korea.jpg
image_caption: Lotus Flower and Seven Treasures Bridges, Bulguksa

title: Seokguram Grotto
creator: kim-dae-seong
location: Mount Toham, Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: An artificial granite grotto housing a seated Buddha, the masterpiece of Silla Buddhist art.
description: Seokguram, built at the same time as Bulguksa and traditionally credited to Kim Dae-seong, translates the cave temples of India and China into a constructed form: since the granite of Mount Toham could not easily be carved, the builders assembled a grotto of cut stone blocks and covered it with earth. A rectangular antechamber and a short corridor lead to a circular rotunda under a dome of stones held by projecting stone 'rivets', in which a seated Buddha more than three metres high faces east towards the sea, surrounded by reliefs of bodhisattvas, disciples and guardians. The geometry of the plan is based on careful proportions. Restorations under Japanese rule in the 1910s used concrete and caused damp problems, and the interior is now behind glass and climate-controlled. It is a World Heritage Site with Bulguksa.
