image_caption: The Buddha of Seokguram seen from the antechamber

title: Muryangsujeon of Buseoksa
creator: korean-temple-carpenters
location: Yeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: One of Korea's oldest wooden halls, celebrated for its entasis columns and mountain setting.
description: Buseoksa was founded in 676 by the monk Uisang, who brought the Hwaeom (Huayan) school of Buddhism from Tang China. Its main hall, the Muryangsujeon, 'Hall of Infinite Life' dedicated to the Buddha Amitabha, was rebuilt in 1376 after a fire, according to an inscription found during repairs, though parts may be older. It is five bays by three, with columns that swell gently in the middle and bracket sets only on the column heads, a simple and dignified structure under a hipped and gabled roof. Inside sits a clay Amitabha facing east, an unusual orientation. The temple is set on terraces on a mountainside with a sweeping view of ranges beyond. It is part of the World Heritage Site of Korean Buddhist mountain monasteries (Sansa).

title: Geungnakjeon of Bongjeongsa
creator: korean-temple-carpenters
location: Andong, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: Probably the oldest surviving wooden building in Korea, a small Goryeo hall.
description: Bongjeongsa is a mountain temple near Andong founded in the late seventh century. Its Geungnakjeon, the 'Hall of Paradise', is a small hall of three bays by four under a gabled roof. A document found during dismantling in 1972 recorded a repair in 1363, implying that the hall was built earlier, probably in the thirteenth century, which makes it the oldest dated timber building in Korea. Its column-head brackets and proportions preserve the style of the Goryeo period. The temple was visited by Queen Elizabeth II in 1999, and it forms part of the Sansa World Heritage Site of Korean Buddhist mountain monasteries.

title: Janggyeong Panjeon of Haeinsa
creator: korean-temple-carpenters
location: Mount Gaya, Hapcheon, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: Naturally ventilated halls that have preserved the 81,258 woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana.
description: The Tripitaka Koreana, the complete Buddhist canon carved on more than 81,000 wooden printing blocks between 1237 and 1248 as a prayer for protection against the Mongols, was moved to Haeinsa in 1398. The present storage halls were built or rebuilt in 1488 under the Joseon dynasty. Four long, plain timber buildings set on the slope are designed to control temperature and humidity naturally: windows of different sizes on the front and back walls, upper and lower, promote air circulation, and the earthen floors contain charcoal, lime and salt to absorb moisture. Modern climate-controlled storage built nearby proved less effective. The blocks have survived war and fire with little damage. The Janggyeong Panjeon became a World Heritage Site in 1995 and the woodblocks are on the Memory of the World register.

title: Gyeongbokgung
creator: joseon-royal-builders
note: The main palace of the Joseon kings, set against Mount Bugak on the axis of the capital.
description: After founding the Joseon dynasty, King Taejo moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul) and in 1395 completed Gyeongbokgung, the 'Palace of Shining Blessings', whose halls were named by the scholar-official Jeong Do-jeon. Laid out to the north of the city on a site chosen by geomancy, with Mount Bugak behind it, it was planned along a north–south axis from the Gwanghwamun gate through courts to the throne hall Geunjeongjeon. The palace burned during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and lay in ruins for over two centuries until the regent Heungseon Daewongun rebuilt it in 1867. Under Japanese rule much of it was demolished and the Government-General building erected in front of the throne hall. That building was removed in 1995–96, and restoration of the palace has continued since 1990. The two-storey Geunjeongjeon and the Gyeonghoeru banquet pavilion on its lotus pond are among the finest Joseon buildings.
image_file: Front view of the Imperial Throne Hall Geunjeongjeon at Gyeongbokgung Palace with blue sky in Seoul.jpg

title: Changdeokgung and its Rear Garden
creator: joseon-royal-builders
note: A Joseon palace fitted to the hills, with the wooded Secret Garden of ponds and pavilions.
description: Changdeokgung was built in 1405 as a secondary palace, and after the destruction of all of Seoul's palaces in 1592 it was the first to be rebuilt, from 1610, serving as the main royal residence for some 270 years. Unlike Gyeongbokgung's formal axis, its buildings are arranged freely to fit the foothills of Mount Bugak. Behind them lies the Rear Garden (Huwon), often called the Secret Garden, which spreads over wooded valleys with ponds, pavilions and halls for study and leisure, such as the Buyongji pond with the Juhamnu library pavilion built under King Jeongjo. The garden shows the Korean preference for working with natural terrain. The palace was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1997.

title: Jongmyo Shrine
creator: joseon-royal-builders
note: The ancestral shrine of the Joseon kings, a single hall of extraordinary length.
description: Jongmyo was built in 1395 to hold the spirit tablets of the Joseon kings and queens, following the Confucian principle that the royal ancestral shrine should stand to the east of the main palace. Burned in 1592, it was rebuilt in 1608, and the main hall, Jeongjeon, was lengthened several times as tablets accumulated, reaching nineteen chambers and a length of about 101 metres; a second hall, Yeongnyeongjeon, holds further tablets. The halls stand on a vast stone terrace, austere and almost unadorned, so that the long, low roof dominates the courtyard. The Jongmyo Jerye ancestral rite, with its court music, is still performed every May. The shrine became a World Heritage Site in 1995, and the rite and music are inscribed as intangible heritage.

title: Sungnyemun (Namdaemun)
creator: joseon-royal-builders
note: The south gate of the Joseon capital, burned by an arsonist in 2008 and rebuilt.
description: Sungnyemun was the main southern gate of the walls of Hanyang, completed in 1398 and rebuilt in 1448. A two-storey timber gate tower under a hipped and gabled roof stands on a massive stone platform with an arched passage. It was the oldest timber structure in Seoul and was designated National Treasure No. 1 in 1962. In February 2008 an arsonist set fire to it and the upper structure was largely destroyed. It was rebuilt by 2013 using traditional tools and methods, including hand-forged nails and roof tiles, and short sections of the city wall on either side were restored. The reconstruction was criticised for some errors, but the loss led to a national debate on heritage protection.

title: Hwaseong Fortress
creator: jeong-yak-yong
note: King Jeongjo's fortress city at Suwon, built with new technology and recorded in a detailed report.
description: King Jeongjo moved the tomb of his father, Crown Prince Sado, to Suwon in 1789 and decided to build a new walled city there, partly as a political base. Jeong Yak-yong planned the fortifications, combining Korean and Chinese practice, and designed lifting devices including the geojunggi crane, which used pulleys to raise heavy stones. Built between 1794 and 1796, the walls run about 5.7 kilometres over hills and plains, with four main gates, sluice gates, command posts, beacon towers and gun emplacements, using both stone and brick. In 1801 a detailed report, the Hwaseong seongyeok uigwe, recorded every stage of construction, with illustrations, costs and the names of workers. When much of the fortress was damaged in the Korean War, this record made its faithful reconstruction possible. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1997.
image_file: Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon, Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea (2).jpg

title: Dosan Seowon
creator: yi-hwang
location: Andong, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: The Confucian academy that grew around Yi Hwang's study hall above the Nakdong River.
description: Yi Hwang built the Dosan Seodang in 1561 as a place to study and teach, and planned it himself: a simple three-bay timber building with a small heated room, a wooden-floored hall and a kitchen, beside a small square lotus pond. After his death his disciples built the Dosan Seowon around it in 1574, with a lecture hall, dormitories for students, a printing block storehouse and a shrine to Yi Hwang at the top of the slope, and King Seonjo granted it a royal charter the following year. The academy's terraces rise up the hillside in an order that expresses the Confucian hierarchy of learning and ritual. It survived the closure of most seowon in 1871 and is one of nine Confucian academies inscribed together as the Seowon World Heritage Site in 2019.

title: Soswaewon
creator: yang-san-bo
location: Damyang, South Jeolla Province, South Korea
note: The most celebrated private garden of Joseon Korea, a scholar's retreat along a mountain stream.
description: Yang San-bo created Soswaewon after withdrawing from public life following the purge of his teacher Jo Gwang-jo in 1519. The garden lies along a small valley where a stream falls over rocks, entered through a bamboo grove. Two pavilions, the Gwangpunggak ('Pavilion of Light and Wind') and the Jewoldang ('Hall of Clear Moon'), are placed to overlook the stream, and an earthen and stone wall, through which the water passes, bends around the slope. Ponds, a wooden water conduit and old trees complete it, with very little alteration of the natural landscape. A woodblock print of 1755 records its forty-eight scenes. Soswaewon was a meeting place for poets of the region and remains the model of the Korean scholar's garden.

title: Hahoe Folk Village
creator: vernacular-builders
location: Andong, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea
note: A village of the Pungsan Ryu clan on a bend of the Nakdong River, with yangban houses and thatched cottages.
description: Hahoe has been the home of the Pungsan Ryu clan since the fifteenth or sixteenth century, and its name refers to the river that winds around it in an S-shaped loop. Large tile-roofed houses of the yangban gentry, arranged in courtyards with separate quarters for men and women, stand among the thatched houses of the commoners who once served them. The village includes a shrine and study halls associated with the statesman Ryu Seong-ryong, chief minister during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s, and Byeongsan Seowon academy lies nearby. Hahoe also preserves a famous masked dance drama. With Yangdong, it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2010 as the Historic Villages of Korea.

title: Kyungdong Presbyterian Church
creator: kim-swoo-geun
note: A fortress-like church of rough brick, Kim Swoo-geun's late meditation on light and enclosure.
description: Kim Swoo-geun designed the Kyungdong Presbyterian Church, completed in 1981, for a congregation in central Seoul. The exterior is a series of massive, fluted brick volumes without obvious windows, built of dark, roughly textured brick, so that the church appears like a closed fortress or a pair of praying hands. Worshippers enter by a long outer stair around the side, and the interior is lit by a concealed skylight above the altar. The building shows Kim's late architecture of brick, intimate passages and controlled light, with its roots in Korean traditional space, and is considered one of the key works of Korean modern architecture.

title: Seoul Olympic Stadium
creator: kim-swoo-geun
note: The main stadium of the 1988 Seoul Olympics, with curves inspired by Joseon porcelain.
description: The Seoul Olympic Stadium, at the Seoul Sports Complex in Jamsil, was designed by Kim Swoo-geun and completed in 1984 as the main venue for the 1986 Asian Games and the 1988 Olympics. Its gently curving roof line, rising and falling around the oval, was inspired by the profile of white porcelain jars of the Joseon period. It seats around 70,000 spectators and was the setting for the opening and closing ceremonies and athletics of the 1988 Games, a key moment in South Korea's emergence on the world stage. Kim died in 1986 before the Games took place.

title: Embassy of France, Seoul
creator: kim-chung-up
note: Kim Chung-up's embassy with soaring concrete roofs evoking Korean eaves.
description: After winning the commission for the French Embassy in Seoul, Kim Chung-up, who had worked in Le Corbusier's studio, designed a complex of buildings completed in 1962 on a hillside. The ambassador's residence and offices are crowned by thin concrete roofs with dramatically upswept corners, a modern reinterpretation of the curved eaves of traditional Korean architecture, set on pilotis among gardens. The building is widely regarded as a landmark of Korean modern architecture, combining Le Corbusier's lessons with a search for national identity. The embassy has since been renovated, with Kim's main buildings kept.
